scenes.tts: Put healthy volunteers in dim light, on a scheduled twenty eight hour day. Their internal day averaged twenty four point one eight hours. That is a study mean, and individuals vary. So what brings the clock back to twenty four, every day?
scenes.caption: Put healthy volunteers in dim light, on a scheduled 28-hour day. Their internal day averaged 24.18 hours. That is a study mean, and individuals vary. So what brings the clock back to 24, every day?
scenes.visual: A 28-hour schedule bar under a dim lamp; the internal-day bar is slightly shorter; a question mark pulls toward 24 h.
scenes.narration: Put healthy volunteers in dim light, on a scheduled 28-hour day. Their internal day averaged 24.18 hours. That is a study mean, and individuals vary. So what brings the clock back to 24, every day?

scenes.tts: In mouse cells, a pair of proteins, CLOCK and BMAL1, binds short DNA sequences called E boxes. That switches on the Per and Cry genes. PER and CRY proteins build up, bind each other, and enter the nucleus. In reporter assays, either CRY one or CRY two abolished CLOCK BMAL1 driven transcription.

scenes.visual: A cell with a nucleus: CLOCK-BMAL1 on an E-box, Per and Cry genes on, PER and CRY accumulate and move in; then in reporter assays CRY1 or CRY2 alone, a red T-bar, transcription abolished.

scenes.tts: As PER and CRY are degraded, the brake comes off, and a new cycle begins. Why does this oscillate, and not settle? Think of a shower with a long pipe. You turn toward hot, nothing changes, and when the hot water arrives, you have overshot. Negative feedback with enough delay keeps overshooting in both directions. Here, transcription, translation, modification, nuclear entry and timed degradation supply hours of delay.

scenes.tts: The loop runs near twenty four hours, not exactly. Take an idealized clock with a period of twenty four point one eight hours. It has no time cues, and starts in phase with the day. Each cycle runs point one eight hours over, which is ten point eight minutes. After seven cycles, its marker falls seventy five point six minutes later than on the day clock.
scenes.caption: The loop runs near 24 hours, not exactly. Take an idealized clock with a period of 24.18 hours. It has no time cues, and starts in phase with the day. Each cycle runs 0.18 hours over, which is 10.8 minutes. After seven cycles, its marker falls 75.6 minutes later than on the 24-hour day.
scenes.visual: The subtraction 24.18 minus 24.00 becomes 10.8 min per cycle; seven bars of growing lag, the last 75.6 min.

scenes.tts: Light must reset the clock, and it reaches the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the S C N, along the retinohypothalamic tract. A tract is a bundle of axons. In isolated rat retina, ganglion cells that project there still depolarized to light, with rod and cone input blocked. They express melanopsin, and rods and cones contribute as well. In the mouse S C N, light pulses strong enough to reset the clock quickly induced Per one transcripts.

scenes.tts: In healthy people under controlled conditions, bright light before the core body temperature minimum delayed the clock. That minimum usually falls in the early morning hours. Light after it advanced the clock. To stay at twenty four hours, this clock needs an average net advance of ten point eight minutes each day. Keep this: the clock runs near a day, and light resets it daily.
